title: Cold open
picture: Boat view, slow dolly; a low close-up of one dimple; a simple cross-section with pressure arrows at a common depth (higher outside, lower toward the centre); restless water; title.
lines: On a quiet stretch of the Rhine, we kept seeing them: small dimples on the water, drifting beside the boat. Some lasted a surprisingly long time.
Each one is the top of a whirlpool.
Spinning water needs an inward push, and pressure provides it: higher outside, lower toward the centre. So above the low-pressure core, the surface dips.
But a river is restless. Everything in it gets sheared and stirred. So what keeps one tiny whirlpool going?

title: 1 · Under the dimple
picture: A dive through the waterline to a translucent tube of spinning water; its axis drawn as a line, with rotation arrows clearly different from the axis. The line meeting the surface in a point. A loop around a whirlpool measuring circulation. The frozen-flow proof: only the measuring loop moves; it keeps its circulation past the imagined end, then shrinks to nothing: contradiction. The tube closing into a ring, or standing on the bed.
lines: Dive under one, and you find a narrow tube of spinning water, reaching down into the river.
Draw a line along its middle, and you have a vortex line. The water turns around it; the line is just how we draw the spin.
A line meets the surface in a single point. That point is the dimple.
In 1858, Hermann von Helmholtz found a strange rule: a tube of spin can't just have a loose end inside the water.
To see why, measure the spin with a loop. Go around it, adding up how fast the water flows along each little piece. That total is the circulation.

Now freeze the flow, and slide the loop along the tube and past its end, never crossing any spinning water. The circulation can't change. But past the end, the loop can shrink to nothing, and nothing has no circulation.
So the tube can't just stop. It has to close into a ring, or end on something: the riverbed, or the surface.

title: 2 · Smoke rings
names: Peter Guthrie Tait and William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin (Edinburgh, 1867); Tait's knot tables; vortex rings reconnecting with a free surface (Bernal and Kwon 1989; Terrington, Hourigan and Thompson 2022)
picture: The tube matched to a smoke ring rolling toward the camera. Tait's box as a simple diagram firing rings. Rings bouncing; one clear leapfrog cycle from the vortex model. A knot turning; a table of knots. A tilted ring rising under the surface, its upper edge arriving first, a glowing reconnection region, leaving a curved tube with two ends. A continuous camera move from two dimples seen from above, down through the surface, to the one connected tube below; hold. The arch with its spin pointing up at one end and down at the other.
lines: A smoke ring is that ring: a tube of spinning air, closed on itself. The smoke lets you see it roll.
In 1867, in Edinburgh, Peter Guthrie Tait showed his smoke rings to his friend William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin.
The rings bounced and wobbled without falling apart. Two rings travelling together can even take turns passing through each other.

Kelvin saw an answer to a much bigger question. In a perfect, frictionless fluid, a ring's circulation would never fade. So maybe atoms were vortex rings in the ether, and each element a different knot.
Kelvin was wrong about atoms. But Tait's attempts to catalogue the knots helped start knot theory.
Now bring a ring up under the water's surface. Tilted, its upper edge arrives first, and it can reconnect to the surface, leaving a curved tube with two ends.
From above, two dimples. From below, one connected tube.
Its spin points up at one end and down at the other, so from above, the two dimples turn opposite ways.

title: 3 · The river's own smoke rings
names: Hairpin vortices in wall turbulence (Theodorsen 1952; Kline and colleagues 1967; Zhou and colleagues 1999); obstacle wakes: a bridge pillar shedding the largest dimples in a photo of the Nidelva (Aarnes, Babiker, Xuan, Shen and Ellingsen 2025); submerged obstacles shedding only in shallow water (Lloyd and Stansby 1997; Shamloo, Rajaratnam and Katopodis 2001); Lake Constance's western arm at a record June low (SRF, 3 June 2026)
picture: A schematic current profile over the bed with one illustrative hairpin rising. The vortex factory: many arches peeling off the bed, most shredded on the way up, one connecting to the surface as a pair. The ideal two-vortex model (labelled) with the pair-speed dial: strengths fixed, separation halved, speed doubled. Then a boulder under the boat-view river shedding a steady, alternating train of dimples from one spot. A cutaway with a water-depth dial: in deep water the rock's arches mostly die before the surface; halve the depth, and upright whirlpools run from bed to surface in two staggered rows.
lines: The Rhine doesn't need a smoke box. The current makes spinning structures for itself.
One source is the riverbed. Friction slows the water nearest the bottom, while the water above keeps gliding along, and that shear rolls up into arches, like half smoke rings.
It happens all the time: the riverbed is a vortex factory. Most arches are torn apart long before they reach the top.
But some rise and connect to the surface, leaving a pair of dimples, turning opposite ways.
Each rides the other's swirl, carrying the pair along. Bring them closer, and they go faster.
A second source is anything that sticks up from the bed: a boulder, a ledge, a bridge pier. Water sweeping past it sheds whirlpools in a steady rhythm, first from one side, then the other.
In one photo of a Norwegian river, the largest dimples had been shed by a bridge pillar. And the shallower the water over a rock, the more of its whirlpools reach the surface.

That spring was so dry that the lake feeding our stretch of the Rhine fell to its lowest June level on record. So were we drifting over the wakes of rocks, closer to the surface than usual? Maybe. Nobody has counted dimples on the Rhine.

title: 4 · What keeps one going
names: Laboratory measurements of surface-attached vortices strengthening in downwellings (Qi, Li and Coletti, J. Fluid Mech. 2025)
picture: First a core spreading, its dimple getting shallower. Then surface water converging and sinking, stretching an upright whirlpool so it spins faster and its dimple deepens, under a surface that stays level. Then ripples added and removed over the same whirlpool, which stays unchanged underneath.
lines: So what keeps a whirlpool going?
Left alone, friction spreads its spin into the water around it. The core widens, and the dimple gets shallower.
But the river can also work the other way. Where surface water converges and sinks, the downward flow stretches an upright whirlpool and spins it faster.
The surface can look perfectly flat while this happens. Flat-looking water isn't the same as water moving only sideways.
So turbulence doesn't only tear whirlpools down. It can also keep them going.
And a dimple can vanish from view before its whirlpool does. Ripples can hide a dimple without destroying the whirlpool underneath.

title: 5 · Reading the river
names: Omer Babiker, Simen Ellingsen and colleagues, NTNU, Trondheim (J. Fluid Mech. 964, R2, 2023; Phys. Rev. Fluids 11, 054802, 2026)
picture: An overhead schematic: dimples counted for the simulation result; then the area covered by dimples and elongated scars highlighted for the laboratory result (labelled schematic, not data). Gases crossing the surface both ways. A bridge-top view of a rock's steady train of dimples. Back to the boat; pull back; end card.
lines: Those hidden motions are exactly what researchers are learning to read from the surface.
A team in Trondheim, Norway, including Omer Babiker and Simen Ellingsen, found in simulations that the number of dimples tracked how strongly the surface was spreading and converging.
This year, laboratory experiments backed up the link, this time measuring the area covered by dimples and by longer marks called scars.
That churning renews the surface, and it helps set how fast gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide cross between water and air.
Crossing a bridge on a calm day, look for a steady beat of whirlpools from one spot. That's a rock, or a pier, writing on the surface.
A dimple isn't a map of everything underneath. But watch one long enough, and you're reading a little of the river below.
